name: Oxyresveratrol

lead: Oxyresveratrol is a natural compound from mulberry and related plants, discussed as a skin-brightening ingredient for dark spots and uneven tone.

Tyrosinase is the enzyme that drives melanin production, and laboratory studies on mushroom and mouse melanoma tyrosinase report potent inhibition by oxyresveratrol, which is the basis for the brightening interest. Other lab and animal studies report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. No human trials of it for pigmentation or skin appearance were found.

paras: It is mentioned as an ingredient for brightening serums and creams. It is reported to be light sensitive and to degrade under UV exposure, so formulation matters.
No human safety data for skin use were found.

angle.text: Discussed as a brightener for dark spots and uneven tone. This mulberry-derived stilbene strongly inhibits tyrosinase in the lab, so less melanin forms. Studies so far are test-tube and animal work.

lead: Oxyresveratrol (2,3',4,5'-tetrahydroxystilbene) is a plant-derived stilbenoid found in species of Morus (mulberry) and Artocarpus, among others [1][2]. It is studied mainly for its strong inhibition of tyrosinase, the enzyme that carries out rate-limiting steps of melanin synthesis, and is therefore discussed as a potential skin-lightening ingredient [3][4].

The evidence for this comes from test-tube and cell work, mostly using mushroom tyrosinase and mouse melanoma cell enzymes [3][4]. Other laboratory and animal studies have reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects [5][6][7]. No human trials of oxyresveratrol for skin appearance were found.

paras: A 1998 study found that oxyresveratrol from Morus alba inhibited the dopa oxidase activity of mushroom tyrosinase in a dose-dependent way, with 50 percent inhibition at roughly 1 micromolar [3]. A 2002 study compared oxyresveratrol and related hydroxystilbenes against mushroom tyrosinase and enzyme from murine B16 melanoma cells, reporting potent inhibition with an IC50 of about 1.2 micromolar on the mushroom enzyme [4]. Structure-activity work on constituents of Morus nigra roots has also examined tyrosinase inhibition by related compounds [8].

Oxyresveratrol has been reported to scavenge free radicals more effectively than resveratrol in an assay using microglial cells [5], to reduce inflammation in rat models [6], and to protect neurons in rodent models of Parkinson-type toxicity and cerebral ischemia [7][9]. Phytochemical surveys list it among mulberry constituents [2].
Wikipedia describes oxyresveratrol as light sensitive, degrading under UV exposure, and as the aglycone of mulberroside A from white mulberry [1].
No studies found. Evidence on oxyresveratrol and pigmentation is limited to in vitro enzyme work and cell and animal research [3][4][6].

timeline.event: Oxyresveratrol is reported as a potent inhibitor of mushroom tyrosinase dopa oxidase activity [3].
Inhibition of mushroom and murine melanoma tyrosinase is characterised for oxyresveratrol and analogs [4].
